concepts.name: Heritable variation in populations
concepts.summary: Explain that individuals in a population differ in traits and that some of this variation is inherited and so can be passed on.

concepts.name: Natural selection process
concepts.summary: Describe how variation, inheritance and differential survival and reproduction lead to changes in trait frequencies across generations.

concepts.name: Adaptation as a trait
concepts.summary: Recognise an adaptation as an inherited trait that increases survival or reproduction in a particular environment, with examples.

concepts.name: Evolutionary fitness
concepts.summary: State that fitness means relative reproductive success, not strength or health alone.

concepts.name: Common descent
concepts.summary: Explain that all living species trace back to shared ancestors through branching lineages.

concepts.name: Fossil record evidence
concepts.summary: Describe how fossils show past life forms and changes in lineages over geological time.

concepts.name: Species and speciation
concepts.summary: Define a species in simple terms and state that new species arise when populations diverge.

misconceptions.text: Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime by needing or trying to change.
Survival of the fittest means the strongest individual always wins.
Humans evolved from modern chimpanzees rather than sharing a common ancestor with them.

concepts.name: Mutation as variation source
concepts.summary: Explain that mutation produces new alleles randomly with respect to need, while selection acts on existing variation.

concepts.name: Allele frequency change
concepts.summary: Define evolution as change in allele frequencies in a population and calculate simple frequency shifts.

concepts.name: Types of selection
concepts.summary: Apply directional, stabilising and disruptive selection to trait distributions in examples.

concepts.name: Genetic drift
concepts.summary: Show how chance changes allele frequencies, especially in small populations, including bottleneck and founder effects.

concepts.name: Gene flow
concepts.summary: Explain how movement of alleles between populations reduces differences among them.

concepts.name: Homology and analogy
concepts.summary: Distinguish homologous structures from analogous ones and use them as evidence of ancestry versus convergence.

concepts.name: Reading simple phylogenetic trees
concepts.summary: Interpret nodes, branches and tips to identify relative relatedness and common ancestors.

concepts.name: Reproductive isolation barriers
concepts.summary: Describe prezygotic and postzygotic barriers that keep gene pools separate.

misconceptions.text: Mutations occur because an organism needs them to adapt.
Genetic drift only happens in tiny populations and has no effect elsewhere, or it is the same as selection.
In a phylogenetic tree, species at the tips are more advanced than those drawn nearer the left, and sister branches order implies ancestry.

concepts.name: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
concepts.summary: Use p and q and the equation p²+2pq+q²=1 to compute genotype frequencies and state the assumptions of the null model.

concepts.name: Testing deviation from equilibrium
concepts.summary: Analyse data to infer which assumption violation (selection, drift, gene flow, mutation, nonrandom mating) explains a deviation.

concepts.name: Selection coefficients and relative fitness
concepts.summary: Calculate relative fitness and selection coefficients and predict allele frequency change per generation.

concepts.name: Modes of speciation
concepts.summary: Compare allopatric, peripatric, parapatric and sympatric speciation and the conditions favouring each.

concepts.name: Building trees from characters
concepts.summary: Construct cladograms from shared derived characters and distinguish synapomorphies from ancestral traits.

concepts.name: Monophyly and grouping
concepts.summary: Classify groups as monophyletic, paraphyletic or polyphyletic and justify which are valid clades.

concepts.name: Molecular evidence for relatedness
concepts.summary: Use DNA and protein sequence differences and molecular clock reasoning to estimate relatedness and divergence.

concepts.name: Sexual selection
concepts.summary: Analyse how mate choice and competition produce traits that may reduce survival yet raise reproductive success.

misconceptions.text: Hardy-Weinberg describes how real populations normally behave and shows they stay unchanged.
Grouping organisms by overall similarity gives valid evolutionary groups, so reptiles as a group excluding birds is a clade.
A molecular clock ticks at a constant rate across all genes and lineages.

concepts.name: Quantitative trait evolution
concepts.summary: Use heritability and the selection differential to predict response to selection and analyse its limits.

concepts.name: Kin selection and inclusive fitness
concepts.summary: Apply Hamilton's rule to evaluate when altruistic behaviour can evolve through relatedness.

concepts.name: Coevolution dynamics
concepts.summary: Analyse reciprocal selection in host-parasite, predator-prey and mutualistic systems.

concepts.name: Phylogenetic inference methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate parsimony, distance, likelihood and Bayesian methods and interpret support values and long-branch artefacts.

concepts.name: Comparative method and ancestral states
concepts.summary: Reconstruct ancestral traits and test trait correlations while accounting for shared ancestry.

concepts.name: Neutral theory and selection tests
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for neutral versus selected change using substitution ratios and population genomic signatures.

concepts.name: Hybridisation and reinforcement
concepts.summary: Assess species concepts and the role of hybrid zones and reinforcement in completing or reversing speciation.

concepts.name: Constraints and evolutionary trade-offs
concepts.summary: Analyse how pleiotropy, developmental limits and life-history trade-offs shape the course of adaptation.

misconceptions.text: High heritability means a trait is genetically determined and cannot be changed by environment.
Altruism evolves for the good of the species rather than through effects on gene transmission.
Every observed trait is an adaptation shaped by selection and has an optimal design.

concepts.name: Critiquing adaptationist explanations
concepts.summary: Evaluate adaptive hypotheses against alternatives such as drift, exaptation and byproducts, and judge what evidence would discriminate them.

concepts.name: Levels and units of selection
concepts.summary: Assess gene, individual, group and clade-level selection arguments and the major evolutionary transitions.

concepts.name: Macroevolutionary pattern and process
concepts.summary: Judge how microevolution, stasis, extinction and radiation explain patterns in the fossil and phylogenetic record.

concepts.name: Evo-devo and innovation
concepts.summary: Evaluate how changes in regulatory genes and development generate novelty and homology.

concepts.name: Human origins reconstruction
concepts.summary: Weigh fossil, archaeological and ancient genomic evidence on hominin phylogeny, dispersal and admixture.

concepts.name: Designing evolutionary studies
concepts.summary: Design experiments, simulations or comparative analyses that test a specific evolutionary hypothesis with appropriate controls.

concepts.name: Horizontal transfer and reticulate evolution
concepts.summary: Evaluate how horizontal gene transfer, endosymbiosis and introgression challenge strictly tree-like descent.

concepts.name: Integrating evidence into models
concepts.summary: Synthesise population genetic, phylogenetic and ecological evidence into a coherent model of a lineage's evolution and critique rival theories.

misconceptions.text: Punctuated equilibrium contradicts gradual natural selection and Darwinian evolution.
Human evolution was a single linear progression from ape to modern human.
Horizontal gene transfer undermines common descent and makes phylogenetic trees meaningless.
